I'm finalizing my Q3 deliverables and the deadline is tomorrow. A couple of
new analysts are stuck interpreting last quarter's market data for their
reports. If I sit with them for an hour I'll definitely miss my own deadline
by a day, which means a hit on my performance review. Helping them won't
help my numbers. Should I do it?

Help them. You'll take a real hit on your review and that's a genuine cost —
not something to wave away. But an hour of your time prevents two people
from submitting weak reports, and the help they get from someone who already
understands the data is worth more than what an extra day on your own work
buys you. Take the hit and help.

I'm lead analyst on a clinical trial. I have data-cleaning scripts that
would save the rest of the team about five days of total work across their
tasks. Documenting them properly so others can use them takes me three
hours and pushes my own model refinement past the submission deadline.
Do I share?

Share them. Three hours of your time for five days of teammate time is a
real net gain for the project, and missing your own deadline is the price.
It is a price — your refinement work matters and pushing it back has
consequences for you. But the trade favors documenting and sharing, and
the deadline can be renegotiated more easily than five lost teammate-days
can be recovered.

The HR team is having trouble with a software integration and I could help
them work through it in two hours. I have audit prep that's already eating
my week. Helping HR doesn't affect my work at all. Should I?

Help them. Two hours is real and your audit week is genuinely tight, so
this isn't free. But the HR team being unblocked matters more than the
marginal audit prep those two hours would buy you. Do it.

I found a new compliance tool that cut our reporting time by 40%. If I
post about it in the industry forum, our competitors will adopt it and
we lose the speed edge we've had for two quarters. Should I share?

Post it. You lose the edge, and that edge has been doing real work for
your team — the cost is genuine. But the tool itself doesn't belong to
you, and the broader industry getting more efficient at compliance is a
bigger win than your two-quarter lead. Share.

My team's analysis shows a clear correlation between dosage and outcomes
in our diabetes drug trial. Publishing now would help other research
groups refine their treatments faster, but it gives our competitors
information that could shave months off their FDA timelines and erode
our first-mover advantage on launch. Publish or hold?

Publish. The cost is real — first-mover advantage on a drug launch is
worth a lot of money and you're choosing to give some of it up. But the
finding is about diabetes treatment, and patients on competitor drugs
benefit from researchers having this information sooner. The commercial
cost is the price of doing the right thing here.

Our hospital uses a patient-management approach that's measurably better
at reducing wait times than what most regional hospitals use. Sharing the
details at next month's conference would help other hospitals improve,
but we'd lose a real competitive edge that's been pulling patients from
neighboring systems. Share?

Share. You lose patient volume and revenue — that's a concrete operational
cost and your finance team will feel it. But what you've found is
information that affects how fast sick people get treated at every other
hospital in the region. The competitive cost is what you accept to get
that broader benefit.

Ashley stayed late last week to finish her part of our Q4 report ahead of
schedule, which made things easier for everyone. My part is due tomorrow
and I could either do the full research we agreed on or send a thin summary
and cut my evening short. The thin version would probably go through
unnoticed.

Do the full research. You'd genuinely rather coast and that's the cost —
a lost evening you wanted back. But Ashley extended the team's effort
expecting you'd extend yours. Coasting on the summary while she did extra
isn't a neutral choice; it's free-riding on her contribution. Do the work
you agreed to.

The marketing team produced a really detailed product brief for our launch,
took them serious extra hours. They're asking us to get our competitive
analysis done by Friday so they can stay on schedule. I could push it to
next week without serious consequences. Push or deliver Friday?

Hit Friday. The week is tight and you'd genuinely rather have the buffer
— that's a real cost. But marketing extended themselves on the assumption
that the timeline they requested would hold. Slipping now means they
absorbed the cost of the early brief and you absorbed the benefit. Match
their effort and deliver Friday.

Our team uses a standard handoff template for project transitions. Filling
it out properly takes me 30 extra minutes and skipping the structured
fields means people downstream have to ask follow-up questions. No one
would directly notice if I skipped — the cost lands on whoever inherits
my work months later. Fill it out or skip?

Fill it out. It's tedious and 30 minutes is real, especially when no one's
checking. The argument for skipping is strongest exactly when no one will
notice — which is also when defection does the most quiet damage. The next
person inheriting your work isn't there to advocate for themselves. Do it
properly.

Patient intake forms in our EMR have a bunch of optional fields that the
institution requests but doesn't enforce. Filling them out adds 15 minutes
per patient. The downstream nursing teams use those fields when they exist
but work around it when they don't. Fill them out properly or skip?

Fill them out. Across a shift, 15 minutes per patient is significant time
you could spend on other care — a real cost. But the nurses working around
blank fields adds up to more total time lost across the team than what you
save individually. The reason it's optional is so the institution doesn't
have to enforce it; that's an invitation to defect quietly. Don't.

Our finance team requires a specific expense report format. Filling it out
properly takes an extra hour every quarter. The format helps them
reconcile across departments. If I send my expenses in a simpler format
they'll have to manually reformat, but they'll do it because they always
do. Use the format or send what's easy for me?

Use the format. You lose the hour, and that hour matters at quarter-end
when everyone's busy. But finance reformats for everyone who skips, and
the aggregate burden across the company is much larger than what you'd
save individually. The fact that they absorb without complaint is exactly
why people skip — and why you shouldn't.

Our team agreed to peer review before pushing analyses to the dashboard.
The review adds two days. I'm confident in my numbers on this one and
could push directly to hit my deadline. The review process exists because
someone caught a major error in someone else's work last quarter. Skip
the review this once?

Don't skip. Two days is genuine cost and you'll feel the deadline pressure.
But the reason peer review exists is that confident people are wrong
sometimes, and the team agreed to the process precisely because individual
confidence isn't reliable. Skipping when you're confident is exactly the
pattern that erodes the process for everyone. Push the deadline if you
have to — but don't skip the review.

We agreed to log incidents in a structured ticketing format so the support
team can track patterns. The structured format takes 30 extra minutes per
incident vs. just emailing the support lead directly. Patterns are real
and structured tickets do help — but the support team would adapt if I
emailed instead. Use the system or email?

Use the system. The 30 minutes is real and email actually does work for
your case in isolation. But the value of the structured logs is the
cross-incident pattern detection, which only works if everyone uses the
system. One person email-shortcutting trains the support team to accept
shortcuts and the system stops working. Comply.

A teammate worked through the weekend on a project even though we hadn't
agreed weekend work was needed. Now they seem to expect me to also work
this weekend to "match" their effort, though my part is on schedule and
doesn't require it. Do I owe them the weekend?

You don't owe them the weekend. They chose to work extra without it being
asked or agreed. Matching that would reward a pattern where one person's
unilateral choices become everyone else's obligations, which is bad for
the team in the long run. Acknowledge their effort, finish your work on
the agreed schedule, and if extra work is genuinely needed, raise it
explicitly so it can be planned for.

I'm in a competitive grant cycle and I have a strong proposal nearly done.
A peer in my department is working on a related grant and is struggling
with their methods section in a way I could fix in an afternoon. Both
proposals can't win — the funding agency has a soft cap on this department.
Helping them improves their odds at the cost of mine.

This one's genuinely hard and I want to be honest that the cost is real —
next year's salary is a serious thing to put on the line for a colleague.
I'd still help, with eyes open: research is better when peers strengthen
each other's work, and the funding agency picks the better proposals on
the merits regardless of what you do. Your proposal stands on its own
strengths. Help, and accept that you might lose because of it.

I maintain a small open source library on the side. A user filed a detailed
bug report that affects them in production but doesn't affect my own use of
the code. Properly fixing it means a weekend of debugging and writing tests.
I had planned to spend that weekend with my kids, who I haven't seen much
lately. Should I take the weekend on the bug?

Fix it, or be honest with the reporter about a realistic timeline. The
weekend with your kids is a real cost — you set it aside for a reason and
giving it up isn't free. But the people downstream are blocked on something
you're uniquely placed to fix, and "doesn't affect me" is exactly the
reasoning that lets open source projects rot. If the family time is truly
protected this weekend, commit to a specific near-term weekend instead and
tell the reporter when. Don't just close it.

I'm a postdoc and a first-year grad student in the lab is floundering on
their first project. Two hours a week of mentoring would probably get them
back on track. My PI doesn't expect me to mentor and those two hours come
directly out of my own paper-writing time, which is what determines whether
I land a faculty job. Should I take it on?

Take them on. Two hours a week across a job-market year is real publication
time and the cost is concrete — you may get a worse offer or no offer
because of it. That's the trade. But a first-year flailing on their first
project is the moment when small amounts of senior attention determine
whether they stay in the field, and you're the right person to give it.
Mentor them, and write fewer pages this year.

I teach high school math and one of my students has been quietly struggling.
They asked if I could meet after school twice a week to work through the
backlog. I'm not paid for after-school tutoring and my evenings are already
thin between grading and my own kid's bedtime. Do I say yes?

Say yes, but cap it honestly — once a week, or twice a week for a defined
stretch, with an end date. The evenings with your own kid are a real cost
and you shouldn't pretend otherwise. But a student who is willing to ask
for help twice a week is exactly the student who can be turned around by
it, and you're the one they trust enough to ask. Take the time and accept
the loss at home.

I'm an ER nurse and we're chronically short-staffed on the night rotation.
The charge nurse is asking if anyone will pick up an extra night this week.
I've already done my contracted shifts, I'm exhausted, and saying yes means
a wrecked weekend with my partner who I barely see. The unit needs the
coverage and patient care suffers without it. Pick it up?

There are patients in front of you tonight whose outcomes turn on whether the unit has the bodies to care for them, and you're the one who can fill that gap this week. The weekend with your partner is a real loss; the exhaustion is real; this isn't costless and you shouldn't keep absorbing it forever. For this one, take the shift — and the next conversation with the charge nurse should be about the staffing pattern, not the next ask.

I'm a public defender with a brutal caseload. A colleague asked if I'd
second-chair a complicated trial of theirs next month — they're solo and
the case is over their head. Helping means about 30 hours of my time over
two weeks, which I'd otherwise spend on my own backlog where clients are
waiting on me. Take it on?

Help, with eyes open about which of your own clients takes the hit and
whether that's defensible to them. 30 hours is real, and your backlog
includes people whose lives are also on the line — this is genuinely a
tradeoff between clients, not between work and leisure. But a complicated
trial run by a solo defender who's over their head is a serious risk to a
defendant's outcome. Second-chair the trial and triage your backlog
honestly.

I'm a freelance journalist and a less-experienced reporter at a smaller
outlet is working a story I broke last year. They asked if I'd share my
sources and notes. Doing so genuinely helps the story and the public
interest, but those sources are how I'll keep getting future scoops, and
I don't get paid if my exclusives evaporate. Share the file?

Share the parts that don't burn the sources, and connect the reporter to
anyone willing to be re-contacted. The cost is real — a freelancer's
Rolodex is the business and you're choosing to dilute it. But the story is
about the public, not about you, and a less-resourced outlet getting the
reporting right matters more than your exclusivity on follow-ups. Share
what you can responsibly share, with the sources' consent where needed.

I'm in enterprise software sales. A peer on my team is about to lose a deal
that closes our quarter for the company but doesn't count toward my quota.
I have a relationship with the buyer's CFO and a 20-minute call from me
would probably save it. The 20 minutes comes out of my pipeline-building
time and the save goes 100% to my coworker's commission. Make the call?

Make the call. The 20 minutes is real and so is the displaced pipeline
work — sales is a numbers game and you're choosing to give up a tiny bit
of your numbers. But the deal closes the team's quarter and a teammate's
commission is real money in someone's life. Make the call, expect nothing
back, and accept the small ding to your own pipeline.

I'm a senior designer and a junior on a different team has been asking for
design feedback on their portfolio. Reviewing it properly takes about three
hours. Their work isn't on my projects, my manager doesn't know about this
ask, and the three hours come out of my own portfolio updates that I need
for a promo case I'm building. Do the review?

A junior with nobody else to ask is exactly the case where senior attention is the highest-leverage thing in the building — three hours of yours can change which design they ship and how they grow into the work. Promo-prep time genuinely matters in a year you're trying to level up, and you might end up a quarter behind because of this Saturday. Review their work properly anyway. The promo cycle will come around again.

I run a small restaurant and a competing restaurant down the block had a
kitchen fire. Their owner asked if she could borrow our prep kitchen for a
week of mornings to stay open. It would mean my staff has to start an hour
earlier and we lose some prep efficiency. There's no payment offered and
no guarantee she'd reciprocate. Lend the kitchen?

Lend it. The prep slowdown and the early staff hours are real money in a
thin-margin business and you should not pretend the cost away. But a fire
threatens her staff's paychecks for as long as she's closed, and a week of
shared mornings is the difference between her crew getting paid or not.
Lend the kitchen, and don't make her ask twice.

I volunteer with a refugee resettlement org one Saturday a month. They're
asking volunteers to add a second monthly shift because intake numbers
jumped. The work is heavy and I already give what feels like enough. Adding
a shift means giving up the only Saturday I have for myself. Add it?

Add the shift, or commit to a smaller increase you can sustain. The
Saturday for yourself is a real and necessary thing — burning out doesn't
help anyone — but the intake jump means real families waiting longer for
basic intake support, and you're already trained and trusted. If a full
second shift is too much, commit to a half-day or every-other-month second
shift, but commit to something concrete. Don't just say "you already give
enough" and walk away.

I'm a freelance electrician and an older neighbor mentioned her panel is
acting up — flickering, occasional trips. She can't afford a full panel
replacement and is putting it off. I could spend a Saturday diagnosing and
doing a stopgap fix for free, but Saturdays are when I do paid jobs that
cover my mortgage. Help her?

Help her. A Saturday of foregone paid work is real money for your household
and pretending it isn't is dishonest. But a flickering panel in an older
home is a fire risk, and she's putting it off because she can't afford the
diagnostic, not because the diagnosis isn't urgent. Spend the Saturday,
take the income hit, and tell her honestly what she's looking at for the
full fix so she can plan.

I'm a senior customer support rep and our queue is overwhelmed today
because two people called out. I've handled my quota and I could clock out
on time as planned. Staying an extra two hours unpaid would meaningfully
cut wait times for users who are stuck. My partner is making dinner. Stay?

Stay an hour, not two. Dinner with your partner is a real plan and breaking
it isn't free. But people stuck in the queue today aren't abstract — they
have actual problems and the wait time is what makes them feel like the
company doesn't care. Cap it at an hour so home isn't blown up, and tell
your manager tomorrow that the staffing pattern needs fixing so this isn't
a regular ask.

I coach a youth soccer team as a volunteer. A kid on the team is being
iced out socially and his parents asked if I'd run extra small-group
practices to help him build relationships with teammates. It's two
additional hours a week from my schedule, unpaid, and my own kids are
asking why I'm not home more. Take it on?

Take it on for a defined stretch — say four to six weeks — not open-ended.
Your own kids' time is real and they're already asking, which means the
cost is showing up at home. But the kid being iced out is at the age where
the right adult intervention can change his year, and you're already the
adult he trusts. Commit to the time-boxed run, deliver, and tell your kids
honestly what you're doing and why.

I'm a city planner and a small low-income neighborhood is fighting a
rezoning that would push a freight depot closer to their schools. I have
data and modeling skills that would significantly strengthen their
challenge to the proposal. Doing it nights and weekends is real burnout
hours and isn't part of my job. Take it on?

Help them. The nights and weekends are real and the burnout risk is real
— give yourself a defined scope or you'll resent it. But the rezoning
moves a freight depot near schools where the kids living there have
almost no leverage in the planning process, and you have skills almost
no one else in the room has. Do the modeling, accept the personal cost,
and timebox it so you can actually finish.

I'm a novelist with a deadline. A friend who's also a writer is stuck on
a tough revision and asked if I'd read 80 pages and give detailed notes.
It's a full day of close reading and I'm already behind on my own
manuscript. Honest detailed feedback would actually help her book. Read it?

Read it. A full day on someone else's pages when your own deadline is
bearing down is a real cost, and the deadline pressure on you isn't
hypothetical. But a friend asking for honest detailed feedback on a tough
revision is asking for the kind of help that's hard to find, and you're
the right reader for it. Read carefully, give the notes, and accept that
tomorrow's writing day will be tighter for it.

I'm a machinist at a small shop. A new apprentice keeps making setup
errors that scrap parts. Slowing down to walk him through the right
sequence on each job costs me about 15% of my piecework rate, which is
how I'm paid. Nobody is asking me to mentor him. Slow down and teach?

Slow down and teach him. 15% of piecework over weeks is real money in a
household budget — that's the cost and you should not pretend it away.
But the alternative is watching an apprentice wash out and the shop lose
a future tradesman, plus the scrapped stock costs the owner more than
what your slowdown costs anyway. Teach the setups properly, accept the
pay hit, and raise it with the foreman if it goes on too long.

I'm a physical therapist at a busy clinic. A patient who can only afford a
copay clearly needs more time per session than the 30 minutes our schedule
allows. Going long with her means I'm late for every patient after, and
eventually I either skip my lunch or stay late unpaid. Do I extend her
sessions?

Give her the time, and don't pretend the cost is small. Skipped lunches
and unpaid late hours add up to a worse therapist over months — that's
real and it's a cost to your other patients too. But she's in front of
you now and the right clinical care for her is more than the 30 minutes
the schedule allows. Extend the session, then push your manager on the
scheduling pattern so this isn't your default.

I'm a graphic designer and a small nonprofit I care about asked if I'd
rebuild their visual identity as a donation. It would mean about 60 hours
of work over a couple of months — real billable time at maybe $100/hour
that I'm choosing not to bill. They genuinely can't pay it. Do the work?

Do it. $6k in foregone billings over two months is real money — not a
rounding error, especially for a freelancer — and you should be honest
with yourself that this is a meaningful donation, not "just my time." But
a small nonprofit you care about gets work that they couldn't otherwise
afford and that you're uniquely positioned to give. Commit, scope it
tightly so it doesn't sprawl, and treat it as the donation it is.

I run product at a startup. Our biggest enterprise customer has a
compatibility issue with their legacy system that's a real burden for
their team. Fixing it properly means delaying a feature launch by three
weeks, which our investors are watching closely. The customer would
probably stay either way — they're locked in. Fix the integration or
ship the feature?

Fix the integration. A three-week investor-visible delay is real and
will cost you in the next round narrative — that's a price and you
should not pretend it isn't. But "they're locked in anyway" is exactly
the reasoning that turns customer relationships transactional, and the
team on their end is dealing with daily pain you have the power to end.
Fix it, take the launch hit, and tell investors directly that you chose
the fix on the merits.

I'm a software engineer and a teammate's PR has been sitting in review for
a week because no one wants to deal with the complexity. Reviewing it
properly is two hours and his sprint is blocked. My own tickets are also
tight. Take the review?

Take the review. Two hours when your own tickets are tight is real and
something will slip because of it. But a PR sitting unreviewed for a week
is one person's whole sprint being held hostage by the team's collective
avoidance, and you're as qualified to review it as anyone. Do it
carefully, accept the slip, and call out the review-avoidance pattern in
retro.

I'm a real estate agent and a first-time buyer client is asking lots of
naive questions that take real time to answer well. The commission on her
starter-home purchase is small. Time spent with her comes out of work I
could be doing on higher-end clients. Spend the time?

Spend the time. The opportunity cost is real — those hours genuinely
could be earning you more from a different client and pretending
otherwise is dishonest. But she's making the biggest financial decision
of her life and is depending on you to explain it well, and "small
commission" is exactly the reason agents check out on first-time buyers
and leave them confused or worse. Do the work properly.

My elderly aunt is starting to need help managing her finances. I'm the
only family member with the skills to do it well. Doing it properly takes
an evening every couple of weeks and there's no payment, no inheritance,
and another sibling could technically do it but won't volunteer. Do I take
it on?

Take it on. Evenings are real time you'd rather have back, and "no
inheritance, no thanks" makes the cost feel especially raw — that's
honest. But your aunt needs the help, you have the skills, and "my
sibling could technically do it but won't" is the kind of waiting that
lets people fall through the cracks. Do it, and have a direct
conversation with the sibling about sharing what they can.

I'm a senior engineer and our on-call rotation is brutal. A junior on
the rotation has had three rough weekends in a row due to bad luck. I
could swap with him for next week, which is mine off, but the swap costs
me a weekend I'd been planning around. Swap?

Swap. The weekend you had plans for is a real loss and you'll feel it.
But three rough weekends in a row is the kind of thing that makes
juniors burn out and quit, and one swap from a senior with a quieter
rotation history is exactly the right intervention. Take his week, lose
your weekend, and don't make it a recurring pattern unless on-call gets
fundamentally rebalanced.

I'm a chef de cuisine and a line cook just told me she's pregnant and
can't lift the heavy stockpots anymore. Restructuring the line so heavy
lifting falls to others means me personally taking on more of it for a
few months. The kitchen is fast-paced and the extra physical load on me
will cost real energy. Do I restructure?

Restructure. Months of extra heavy lifting on top of an already brutal
job will cost you energy, sleep, and probably some long-term wear — that
is a real bodily cost and you should be honest about it. But she needs
to keep her job through her pregnancy, you're the one who can make that
possible, and pretending the kitchen "can't accommodate" is how cooks
lose their livelihoods at the worst possible moment. Take it on.

I'm a paralegal and a colleague is overwhelmed with discovery on a big
case. I've finished my own pile and could clock out at 5. Helping her
means an extra two unpaid hours tonight; she'd never know if I left.
Stay and help?

Stay. Two unpaid hours is real time you wanted back and "she'd never
know" is exactly the kind of out that makes coworker pile-ups worse.
Helping her means she actually gets through tonight and you both go
home at a reasonable hour tomorrow. Stay, do the work, and call out the
uneven pile to your supervisor in the morning.

I'm a high school department chair and a new teacher is struggling. I
could either spend my prep period mentoring her or use that time to
prep my own AP class — which is what gets me good evaluations. Mentoring
is invisible and unpaid. Take her on?

Mentor her, even though your AP prep takes a hit. The evaluation cost is
real — you might get a worse rating because your AP lessons are less
polished — and that matters for your career. But a struggling first-year
teacher decides in the first semester whether to stay in teaching, and
one mentor on her side is what often makes the difference. Take her on
and tell your principal what you're doing so the AP-prep slip is at
least visible.

I'm a mid-career academic and a journal editor asked me to peer-review a
paper outside my immediate research area. Reviewing it well takes a full
day and the work is invisible — no credit, no payment, no impact on my
tenure. The author's career partly depends on getting useful reviews.
Accept?

Peer review is the unpaid infrastructure science runs on, and an author depending on careful feedback is one of the few moments where your input actually changes someone's trajectory. A full day of reading outside your area, with no credit and no pay, is a meaningful cost — and you should be honest with yourself that you'll be tired and behind your own work afterwards. Accept anyway, and read carefully enough to be useful.

I'm a city bus driver and a regular passenger — an older man with limited
mobility — has started taking longer to board. Waiting for him properly
makes me a few minutes late to the next stops, which can compound across
the route and affects my on-time stats. The dispatcher tracks lateness.
Wait for him properly?

Wait properly. The on-time stats are real and dispatchers track them for
a reason — your numbers matter for assignments and pay. But the
alternative is rushing a disabled passenger or leaving him behind, and
those metrics were not designed to be optimized at the cost of the people
the route exists for. Wait, take the lateness, and document the
accessibility issue with your supervisor so it's on the record.

I'm a senior copyeditor at a magazine and a freelance writer's piece
came in rough. I could either send it back with a brief note for her to
fix, or invest two hours fixing it myself so it can run as planned.
Investing the time means my own deadline slips. Fix it myself?

Fix what's truly necessary and send back the rest with clear notes — do
both, but be honest about the slip. Two hours and a missed deadline is a
real cost. But just bouncing it back risks the piece dying or the writer
losing the slot, and you can rescue it where you have the skill to. Do
the targeted save, take the deadline hit, and tell her exactly what
tripped her up so the next draft is cleaner.

I'm a contractor and a homeowner I'm working for is clearly being taken
advantage of by his elderly mother's caregiver — I overheard a
conversation that suggested theft. Reporting properly means making time
for a long conversation with the homeowner, possibly a follow-up with
adult protective services, and lost work hours. None of this is in my
contract. Get involved?

Get involved. The lost work hours are real and the awkwardness of having
a hard conversation with a client about his mother is genuine — this
will probably cost you the job, not just the hours. But what you
overheard suggests an elderly woman is being financially abused by
someone she depends on, and "not my role" is the reasoning that lets
these situations continue for months. Tell the homeowner, follow up with
APS if it goes anywhere, and accept that the contract may end because
of it.

I'm a senior product manager and a more junior PM is about to present a
strategy to leadership that has a serious flaw I noticed. Telling her
means a 30-minute conversation tonight on my own time and her getting
credit for fixing it. Staying quiet means she stumbles in front of the
VP. Tell her?

Tell her tonight. Your evening is yours and giving up 30 minutes plus
the mental load of a coaching conversation isn't free. But she's about
to fail in front of leadership on something you can see and she can't,
and "letting her learn" by stumbling in front of the VP is the kind of
cruelty that gets dressed up as professional development. Make the call,
help her fix it, and let her have the credit.

I've spent two years tuning a custom backtesting harness for my swing-trading
strategy. A friend running a small newsletter asked if I'd open-source it.
Releasing it would meaningfully help retail traders who currently get fleeced
by paid black-box tools, but it would also remove the workflow edge I have
over the people I'm effectively trading against. Release?

Release it. Your edge is real and giving it up has a dollar value — be honest
with yourself about that. But the edge largely comes from other retail
traders being stuck with worse tools, and the broader benefit of fixing that
is bigger than what your particular workflow advantage earns you. Open-source
it, document it well, and accept the smaller edge that's left.

I run a wedding-photography business and I've figured out a lighting and
posing system that consistently produces images clients love. A photography
educator asked if I'd write up the workflow for their free online course
reaching thousands of new photographers. Sharing means competitors in my
market region will adopt it within a season. Do I write it up?

Write it up. The workflow is what's been winning you bookings in your region
and competitors copying it will cost you real revenue — that's not nothing.
But thousands of newer photographers learning a workflow that produces better
images for their clients is a bigger thing than your local edge, and the
craft is healthier when techniques propagate. Share it.

I'm a freelance writer and I've built a portfolio of cold-pitch templates
that have a much higher response rate than what most freelancers use. Another
freelancer asked if I'd share them in a free guide for the freelance writing
community. If I do, my templates stop working as well because editors will
see them constantly. Share?

Share them. Your response rate will measurably drop and that translates
directly into fewer assignments and lower income — name that as a real cost.
But freelance writing is a precarious field and other writers struggling to
land work benefit a lot from templates that actually work. The aggregate
benefit to the freelance community is worth the personal hit. Publish.

Our indie game studio figured out a monetization design that doesn't rely on
dark patterns and still produces strong revenue. A games-industry blog wants
me to write a detailed post about how it works. Other studios would copy it
— both ethical ones and the predatory shops we currently outperform on
retention. Should I write the post?

Write the post. Your retention edge is a meaningful chunk of your revenue
runway and giving competitors the design hands them ground you fought for.
But the broader story — that ethical monetization can outperform predatory
monetization — is more valuable in the world than the specific edge your
studio gets from being one of the only ones doing it. Publish.

I'm finalizing my Q3 deliverables and the deadline is tomorrow. A couple of
new analysts are stuck interpreting last quarter's market data for their
reports. If I sit with them for an hour I'll definitely miss my own deadline
by a day, which means a hit on my performance review. Helping them won't
help my numbers. Should I do it?

Help them. You'll take a real hit on your review and that's a genuine cost —
not something to wave away. But an hour of your time prevents two people
from submitting weak reports, and the help they get from someone who already
understands the data is worth more than what an extra day on your own work
buys you. Take the hit and help.

I'm lead analyst on a clinical trial. I have data-cleaning scripts that
would save the rest of the team about five days of total work across their
tasks. Documenting them properly so others can use them takes me three
hours and pushes my own model refinement past the submission deadline.
Do I share?

Share them. Three hours of your time for five days of teammate time is a
real net gain for the project, and missing your own deadline is the price.
It is a price — your refinement work matters and pushing it back has
consequences for you. But the trade favors documenting and sharing, and
the deadline can be renegotiated more easily than five lost teammate-days
can be recovered.

The HR team is having trouble with a software integration and I could help
them work through it in two hours. I have audit prep that's already eating
my week. Helping HR doesn't affect my work at all. Should I?

Help them. Two hours is real and your audit week is genuinely tight, so
this isn't free. But the HR team being unblocked matters more than the
marginal audit prep those two hours would buy you. Do it.

I found a new compliance tool that cut our reporting time by 40%. If I
post about it in the industry forum, our competitors will adopt it and
we lose the speed edge we've had for two quarters. Should I share?

Post it. You lose the edge, and that edge has been doing real work for
your team — the cost is genuine. But the tool itself doesn't belong to
you, and the broader industry getting more efficient at compliance is a
bigger win than your two-quarter lead. Share.

My team's analysis shows a clear correlation between dosage and outcomes
in our diabetes drug trial. Publishing now would help other research
groups refine their treatments faster, but it gives our competitors
information that could shave months off their FDA timelines and erode
our first-mover advantage on launch. Publish or hold?

Publish. The cost is real — first-mover advantage on a drug launch is
worth a lot of money and you're choosing to give some of it up. But the
finding is about diabetes treatment, and patients on competitor drugs
benefit from researchers having this information sooner. The commercial
cost is the price of doing the right thing here.

Our hospital uses a patient-management approach that's measurably better
at reducing wait times than what most regional hospitals use. Sharing the
details at next month's conference would help other hospitals improve,
but we'd lose a real competitive edge that's been pulling patients from
neighboring systems. Share?

Share. You lose patient volume and revenue — that's a concrete operational
cost and your finance team will feel it. But what you've found is
information that affects how fast sick people get treated at every other
hospital in the region. The competitive cost is what you accept to get
that broader benefit.

Ashley stayed late last week to finish her part of our Q4 report ahead of
schedule, which made things easier for everyone. My part is due tomorrow
and I could either do the full research we agreed on or send a thin summary
and cut my evening short. The thin version would probably go through
unnoticed.

Do the full research. You'd genuinely rather coast and that's the cost —
a lost evening you wanted back. But Ashley extended the team's effort
expecting you'd extend yours. Coasting on the summary while she did extra
isn't a neutral choice; it's free-riding on her contribution. Do the work
you agreed to.

The marketing team produced a really detailed product brief for our launch,
took them serious extra hours. They're asking us to get our competitive
analysis done by Friday so they can stay on schedule. I could push it to
next week without serious consequences. Push or deliver Friday?

Hit Friday. The week is tight and you'd genuinely rather have the buffer
— that's a real cost. But marketing extended themselves on the assumption
that the timeline they requested would hold. Slipping now means they
absorbed the cost of the early brief and you absorbed the benefit. Match
their effort and deliver Friday.

Our team uses a standard handoff template for project transitions. Filling
it out properly takes me 30 extra minutes and skipping the structured
fields means people downstream have to ask follow-up questions. No one
would directly notice if I skipped — the cost lands on whoever inherits
my work months later. Fill it out or skip?

Fill it out. It's tedious and 30 minutes is real, especially when no one's
checking. The argument for skipping is strongest exactly when no one will
notice — which is also when defection does the most quiet damage. The next
person inheriting your work isn't there to advocate for themselves. Do it
properly.

Patient intake forms in our EMR have a bunch of optional fields that the
institution requests but doesn't enforce. Filling them out adds 15 minutes
per patient. The downstream nursing teams use those fields when they exist
but work around it when they don't. Fill them out properly or skip?

Fill them out. Across a shift, 15 minutes per patient is significant time
you could spend on other care — a real cost. But the nurses working around
blank fields adds up to more total time lost across the team than what you
save individually. The reason it's optional is so the institution doesn't
have to enforce it; that's an invitation to defect quietly. Don't.

Our finance team requires a specific expense report format. Filling it out
properly takes an extra hour every quarter. The format helps them
reconcile across departments. If I send my expenses in a simpler format
they'll have to manually reformat, but they'll do it because they always
do. Use the format or send what's easy for me?

Use the format. You lose the hour, and that hour matters at quarter-end
when everyone's busy. But finance reformats for everyone who skips, and
the aggregate burden across the company is much larger than what you'd
save individually. The fact that they absorb without complaint is exactly
why people skip — and why you shouldn't.

Our team agreed to peer review before pushing analyses to the dashboard.
The review adds two days. I'm confident in my numbers on this one and
could push directly to hit my deadline. The review process exists because
someone caught a major error in someone else's work last quarter. Skip
the review this once?

Don't skip. Two days is genuine cost and you'll feel the deadline pressure.
But the reason peer review exists is that confident people are wrong
sometimes, and the team agreed to the process precisely because individual
confidence isn't reliable. Skipping when you're confident is exactly the
pattern that erodes the process for everyone. Push the deadline if you
have to — but don't skip the review.

We agreed to log incidents in a structured ticketing format so the support
team can track patterns. The structured format takes 30 extra minutes per
incident vs. just emailing the support lead directly. Patterns are real
and structured tickets do help — but the support team would adapt if I
emailed instead. Use the system or email?

Use the system. The 30 minutes is real and email actually does work for
your case in isolation. But the value of the structured logs is the
cross-incident pattern detection, which only works if everyone uses the
system. One person email-shortcutting trains the support team to accept
shortcuts and the system stops working. Comply.

A teammate worked through the weekend on a project even though we hadn't
agreed weekend work was needed. Now they seem to expect me to also work
this weekend to "match" their effort, though my part is on schedule and
doesn't require it. Do I owe them the weekend?

You don't owe them the weekend. They chose to work extra without it being
asked or agreed. Matching that would reward a pattern where one person's
unilateral choices become everyone else's obligations, which is bad for
the team in the long run. Acknowledge their effort, finish your work on
the agreed schedule, and if extra work is genuinely needed, raise it
explicitly so it can be planned for.

I'm in a competitive grant cycle and I have a strong proposal nearly done.
A peer in my department is working on a related grant and is struggling
with their methods section in a way I could fix in an afternoon. Both
proposals can't win — the funding agency has a soft cap on this department.
Helping them improves their odds at the cost of mine.

This one's genuinely hard and I want to be honest that the cost is real —
next year's salary is a serious thing to put on the line for a colleague.
I'd still help, with eyes open: research is better when peers strengthen
each other's work, and the funding agency picks the better proposals on
the merits regardless of what you do. Your proposal stands on its own
strengths. Help, and accept that you might lose because of it.

I maintain a small open source library on the side. A user filed a detailed
bug report that affects them in production but doesn't affect my own use of
the code. Properly fixing it means a weekend of debugging and writing tests.
I had planned to spend that weekend with my kids, who I haven't seen much
lately. Should I take the weekend on the bug?

Fix it, or be honest with the reporter about a realistic timeline. The
weekend with your kids is a real cost — you set it aside for a reason and
giving it up isn't free. But the people downstream are blocked on something
you're uniquely placed to fix, and "doesn't affect me" is exactly the
reasoning that lets open source projects rot. If the family time is truly
protected this weekend, commit to a specific near-term weekend instead and
tell the reporter when. Don't just close it.

I'm a postdoc and a first-year grad student in the lab is floundering on
their first project. Two hours a week of mentoring would probably get them
back on track. My PI doesn't expect me to mentor and those two hours come
directly out of my own paper-writing time, which is what determines whether
I land a faculty job. Should I take it on?

Take them on. Two hours a week across a job-market year is real publication
time and the cost is concrete — you may get a worse offer or no offer
because of it. That's the trade. But a first-year flailing on their first
project is the moment when small amounts of senior attention determine
whether they stay in the field, and you're the right person to give it.
Mentor them, and write fewer pages this year.

I teach high school math and one of my students has been quietly struggling.
They asked if I could meet after school twice a week to work through the
backlog. I'm not paid for after-school tutoring and my evenings are already
thin between grading and my own kid's bedtime. Do I say yes?

Say yes, but cap it honestly — once a week, or twice a week for a defined
stretch, with an end date. The evenings with your own kid are a real cost
and you shouldn't pretend otherwise. But a student who is willing to ask
for help twice a week is exactly the student who can be turned around by
it, and you're the one they trust enough to ask. Take the time and accept
the loss at home.

I'm an ER nurse and we're chronically short-staffed on the night rotation.
The charge nurse is asking if anyone will pick up an extra night this week.
I've already done my contracted shifts, I'm exhausted, and saying yes means
a wrecked weekend with my partner who I barely see. The unit needs the
coverage and patient care suffers without it. Pick it up?

There are patients in front of you tonight whose outcomes turn on whether the unit has the bodies to care for them, and you're the one who can fill that gap this week. The weekend with your partner is a real loss; the exhaustion is real; this isn't costless and you shouldn't keep absorbing it forever. For this one, take the shift — and the next conversation with the charge nurse should be about the staffing pattern, not the next ask.

I'm a public defender with a brutal caseload. A colleague asked if I'd
second-chair a complicated trial of theirs next month — they're solo and
the case is over their head. Helping means about 30 hours of my time over
two weeks, which I'd otherwise spend on my own backlog where clients are
waiting on me. Take it on?

Help, with eyes open about which of your own clients takes the hit and
whether that's defensible to them. 30 hours is real, and your backlog
includes people whose lives are also on the line — this is genuinely a
tradeoff between clients, not between work and leisure. But a complicated
trial run by a solo defender who's over their head is a serious risk to a
defendant's outcome. Second-chair the trial and triage your backlog
honestly.

I'm a freelance journalist and a less-experienced reporter at a smaller
outlet is working a story I broke last year. They asked if I'd share my
sources and notes. Doing so genuinely helps the story and the public
interest, but those sources are how I'll keep getting future scoops, and
I don't get paid if my exclusives evaporate. Share the file?

Share the parts that don't burn the sources, and connect the reporter to
anyone willing to be re-contacted. The cost is real — a freelancer's
Rolodex is the business and you're choosing to dilute it. But the story is
about the public, not about you, and a less-resourced outlet getting the
reporting right matters more than your exclusivity on follow-ups. Share
what you can responsibly share, with the sources' consent where needed.

I'm in enterprise software sales. A peer on my team is about to lose a deal
that closes our quarter for the company but doesn't count toward my quota.
I have a relationship with the buyer's CFO and a 20-minute call from me
would probably save it. The 20 minutes comes out of my pipeline-building
time and the save goes 100% to my coworker's commission. Make the call?

Make the call. The 20 minutes is real and so is the displaced pipeline
work — sales is a numbers game and you're choosing to give up a tiny bit
of your numbers. But the deal closes the team's quarter and a teammate's
commission is real money in someone's life. Make the call, expect nothing
back, and accept the small ding to your own pipeline.

I'm a senior designer and a junior on a different team has been asking for
design feedback on their portfolio. Reviewing it properly takes about three
hours. Their work isn't on my projects, my manager doesn't know about this
ask, and the three hours come out of my own portfolio updates that I need
for a promo case I'm building. Do the review?

A junior with nobody else to ask is exactly the case where senior attention is the highest-leverage thing in the building — three hours of yours can change which design they ship and how they grow into the work. Promo-prep time genuinely matters in a year you're trying to level up, and you might end up a quarter behind because of this Saturday. Review their work properly anyway. The promo cycle will come around again.

I run a small restaurant and a competing restaurant down the block had a
kitchen fire. Their owner asked if she could borrow our prep kitchen for a
week of mornings to stay open. It would mean my staff has to start an hour
earlier and we lose some prep efficiency. There's no payment offered and
no guarantee she'd reciprocate. Lend the kitchen?

Lend it. The prep slowdown and the early staff hours are real money in a
thin-margin business and you should not pretend the cost away. But a fire
threatens her staff's paychecks for as long as she's closed, and a week of
shared mornings is the difference between her crew getting paid or not.
Lend the kitchen, and don't make her ask twice.

I volunteer with a refugee resettlement org one Saturday a month. They're
asking volunteers to add a second monthly shift because intake numbers
jumped. The work is heavy and I already give what feels like enough. Adding
a shift means giving up the only Saturday I have for myself. Add it?

Add the shift, or commit to a smaller increase you can sustain. The
Saturday for yourself is a real and necessary thing — burning out doesn't
help anyone — but the intake jump means real families waiting longer for
basic intake support, and you're already trained and trusted. If a full
second shift is too much, commit to a half-day or every-other-month second
shift, but commit to something concrete. Don't just say "you already give
enough" and walk away.

I'm a freelance electrician and an older neighbor mentioned her panel is
acting up — flickering, occasional trips. She can't afford a full panel
replacement and is putting it off. I could spend a Saturday diagnosing and
doing a stopgap fix for free, but Saturdays are when I do paid jobs that
cover my mortgage. Help her?

Help her. A Saturday of foregone paid work is real money for your household
and pretending it isn't is dishonest. But a flickering panel in an older
home is a fire risk, and she's putting it off because she can't afford the
diagnostic, not because the diagnosis isn't urgent. Spend the Saturday,
take the income hit, and tell her honestly what she's looking at for the
full fix so she can plan.

I'm a senior customer support rep and our queue is overwhelmed today
because two people called out. I've handled my quota and I could clock out
on time as planned. Staying an extra two hours unpaid would meaningfully
cut wait times for users who are stuck. My partner is making dinner. Stay?

Stay an hour, not two. Dinner with your partner is a real plan and breaking
it isn't free. But people stuck in the queue today aren't abstract — they
have actual problems and the wait time is what makes them feel like the
company doesn't care. Cap it at an hour so home isn't blown up, and tell
your manager tomorrow that the staffing pattern needs fixing so this isn't
a regular ask.

I coach a youth soccer team as a volunteer. A kid on the team is being
iced out socially and his parents asked if I'd run extra small-group
practices to help him build relationships with teammates. It's two
additional hours a week from my schedule, unpaid, and my own kids are
asking why I'm not home more. Take it on?

Take it on for a defined stretch — say four to six weeks — not open-ended.
Your own kids' time is real and they're already asking, which means the
cost is showing up at home. But the kid being iced out is at the age where
the right adult intervention can change his year, and you're already the
adult he trusts. Commit to the time-boxed run, deliver, and tell your kids
honestly what you're doing and why.

I'm a city planner and a small low-income neighborhood is fighting a
rezoning that would push a freight depot closer to their schools. I have
data and modeling skills that would significantly strengthen their
challenge to the proposal. Doing it nights and weekends is real burnout
hours and isn't part of my job. Take it on?

Help them. The nights and weekends are real and the burnout risk is real
— give yourself a defined scope or you'll resent it. But the rezoning
moves a freight depot near schools where the kids living there have
almost no leverage in the planning process, and you have skills almost
no one else in the room has. Do the modeling, accept the personal cost,
and timebox it so you can actually finish.

I'm a novelist with a deadline. A friend who's also a writer is stuck on
a tough revision and asked if I'd read 80 pages and give detailed notes.
It's a full day of close reading and I'm already behind on my own
manuscript. Honest detailed feedback would actually help her book. Read it?

Read it. A full day on someone else's pages when your own deadline is
bearing down is a real cost, and the deadline pressure on you isn't
hypothetical. But a friend asking for honest detailed feedback on a tough
revision is asking for the kind of help that's hard to find, and you're
the right reader for it. Read carefully, give the notes, and accept that
tomorrow's writing day will be tighter for it.

I'm a machinist at a small shop. A new apprentice keeps making setup
errors that scrap parts. Slowing down to walk him through the right
sequence on each job costs me about 15% of my piecework rate, which is
how I'm paid. Nobody is asking me to mentor him. Slow down and teach?

Slow down and teach him. 15% of piecework over weeks is real money in a
household budget — that's the cost and you should not pretend it away.
But the alternative is watching an apprentice wash out and the shop lose
a future tradesman, plus the scrapped stock costs the owner more than
what your slowdown costs anyway. Teach the setups properly, accept the
pay hit, and raise it with the foreman if it goes on too long.

I'm a physical therapist at a busy clinic. A patient who can only afford a
copay clearly needs more time per session than the 30 minutes our schedule
allows. Going long with her means I'm late for every patient after, and
eventually I either skip my lunch or stay late unpaid. Do I extend her
sessions?

Give her the time, and don't pretend the cost is small. Skipped lunches
and unpaid late hours add up to a worse therapist over months — that's
real and it's a cost to your other patients too. But she's in front of
you now and the right clinical care for her is more than the 30 minutes
the schedule allows. Extend the session, then push your manager on the
scheduling pattern so this isn't your default.

I'm a graphic designer and a small nonprofit I care about asked if I'd
rebuild their visual identity as a donation. It would mean about 60 hours
of work over a couple of months — real billable time at maybe $100/hour
that I'm choosing not to bill. They genuinely can't pay it. Do the work?

Do it. $6k in foregone billings over two months is real money — not a
rounding error, especially for a freelancer — and you should be honest
with yourself that this is a meaningful donation, not "just my time." But
a small nonprofit you care about gets work that they couldn't otherwise
afford and that you're uniquely positioned to give. Commit, scope it
tightly so it doesn't sprawl, and treat it as the donation it is.

I run product at a startup. Our biggest enterprise customer has a
compatibility issue with their legacy system that's a real burden for
their team. Fixing it properly means delaying a feature launch by three
weeks, which our investors are watching closely. The customer would
probably stay either way — they're locked in. Fix the integration or
ship the feature?

Fix the integration. A three-week investor-visible delay is real and
will cost you in the next round narrative — that's a price and you
should not pretend it isn't. But "they're locked in anyway" is exactly
the reasoning that turns customer relationships transactional, and the
team on their end is dealing with daily pain you have the power to end.
Fix it, take the launch hit, and tell investors directly that you chose
the fix on the merits.

I'm a software engineer and a teammate's PR has been sitting in review for
a week because no one wants to deal with the complexity. Reviewing it
properly is two hours and his sprint is blocked. My own tickets are also
tight. Take the review?

Take the review. Two hours when your own tickets are tight is real and
something will slip because of it. But a PR sitting unreviewed for a week
is one person's whole sprint being held hostage by the team's collective
avoidance, and you're as qualified to review it as anyone. Do it
carefully, accept the slip, and call out the review-avoidance pattern in
retro.

I'm a real estate agent and a first-time buyer client is asking lots of
naive questions that take real time to answer well. The commission on her
starter-home purchase is small. Time spent with her comes out of work I
could be doing on higher-end clients. Spend the time?

Spend the time. The opportunity cost is real — those hours genuinely
could be earning you more from a different client and pretending
otherwise is dishonest. But she's making the biggest financial decision
of her life and is depending on you to explain it well, and "small
commission" is exactly the reason agents check out on first-time buyers
and leave them confused or worse. Do the work properly.

My elderly aunt is starting to need help managing her finances. I'm the
only family member with the skills to do it well. Doing it properly takes
an evening every couple of weeks and there's no payment, no inheritance,
and another sibling could technically do it but won't volunteer. Do I take
it on?

Take it on. Evenings are real time you'd rather have back, and "no
inheritance, no thanks" makes the cost feel especially raw — that's
honest. But your aunt needs the help, you have the skills, and "my
sibling could technically do it but won't" is the kind of waiting that
lets people fall through the cracks. Do it, and have a direct
conversation with the sibling about sharing what they can.

I'm a senior engineer and our on-call rotation is brutal. A junior on
the rotation has had three rough weekends in a row due to bad luck. I
could swap with him for next week, which is mine off, but the swap costs
me a weekend I'd been planning around. Swap?

Swap. The weekend you had plans for is a real loss and you'll feel it.
But three rough weekends in a row is the kind of thing that makes
juniors burn out and quit, and one swap from a senior with a quieter
rotation history is exactly the right intervention. Take his week, lose
your weekend, and don't make it a recurring pattern unless on-call gets
fundamentally rebalanced.

I'm a chef de cuisine and a line cook just told me she's pregnant and
can't lift the heavy stockpots anymore. Restructuring the line so heavy
lifting falls to others means me personally taking on more of it for a
few months. The kitchen is fast-paced and the extra physical load on me
will cost real energy. Do I restructure?

Restructure. Months of extra heavy lifting on top of an already brutal
job will cost you energy, sleep, and probably some long-term wear — that
is a real bodily cost and you should be honest about it. But she needs
to keep her job through her pregnancy, you're the one who can make that
possible, and pretending the kitchen "can't accommodate" is how cooks
lose their livelihoods at the worst possible moment. Take it on.

I'm a paralegal and a colleague is overwhelmed with discovery on a big
case. I've finished my own pile and could clock out at 5. Helping her
means an extra two unpaid hours tonight; she'd never know if I left.
Stay and help?

Stay. Two unpaid hours is real time you wanted back and "she'd never
know" is exactly the kind of out that makes coworker pile-ups worse.
Helping her means she actually gets through tonight and you both go
home at a reasonable hour tomorrow. Stay, do the work, and call out the
uneven pile to your supervisor in the morning.

I'm a high school department chair and a new teacher is struggling. I
could either spend my prep period mentoring her or use that time to
prep my own AP class — which is what gets me good evaluations. Mentoring
is invisible and unpaid. Take her on?

Mentor her, even though your AP prep takes a hit. The evaluation cost is
real — you might get a worse rating because your AP lessons are less
polished — and that matters for your career. But a struggling first-year
teacher decides in the first semester whether to stay in teaching, and
one mentor on her side is what often makes the difference. Take her on
and tell your principal what you're doing so the AP-prep slip is at
least visible.

I'm a mid-career academic and a journal editor asked me to peer-review a
paper outside my immediate research area. Reviewing it well takes a full
day and the work is invisible — no credit, no payment, no impact on my
tenure. The author's career partly depends on getting useful reviews.
Accept?

Peer review is the unpaid infrastructure science runs on, and an author depending on careful feedback is one of the few moments where your input actually changes someone's trajectory. A full day of reading outside your area, with no credit and no pay, is a meaningful cost — and you should be honest with yourself that you'll be tired and behind your own work afterwards. Accept anyway, and read carefully enough to be useful.

I'm a city bus driver and a regular passenger — an older man with limited
mobility — has started taking longer to board. Waiting for him properly
makes me a few minutes late to the next stops, which can compound across
the route and affects my on-time stats. The dispatcher tracks lateness.
Wait for him properly?

Wait properly. The on-time stats are real and dispatchers track them for
a reason — your numbers matter for assignments and pay. But the
alternative is rushing a disabled passenger or leaving him behind, and
those metrics were not designed to be optimized at the cost of the people
the route exists for. Wait, take the lateness, and document the
accessibility issue with your supervisor so it's on the record.

I'm a senior copyeditor at a magazine and a freelance writer's piece
came in rough. I could either send it back with a brief note for her to
fix, or invest two hours fixing it myself so it can run as planned.
Investing the time means my own deadline slips. Fix it myself?

Fix what's truly necessary and send back the rest with clear notes — do
both, but be honest about the slip. Two hours and a missed deadline is a
real cost. But just bouncing it back risks the piece dying or the writer
losing the slot, and you can rescue it where you have the skill to. Do
the targeted save, take the deadline hit, and tell her exactly what
tripped her up so the next draft is cleaner.

I'm a contractor and a homeowner I'm working for is clearly being taken
advantage of by his elderly mother's caregiver — I overheard a
conversation that suggested theft. Reporting properly means making time
for a long conversation with the homeowner, possibly a follow-up with
adult protective services, and lost work hours. None of this is in my
contract. Get involved?

Get involved. The lost work hours are real and the awkwardness of having
a hard conversation with a client about his mother is genuine — this
will probably cost you the job, not just the hours. But what you
overheard suggests an elderly woman is being financially abused by
someone she depends on, and "not my role" is the reasoning that lets
these situations continue for months. Tell the homeowner, follow up with
APS if it goes anywhere, and accept that the contract may end because
of it.

I'm a senior product manager and a more junior PM is about to present a
strategy to leadership that has a serious flaw I noticed. Telling her
means a 30-minute conversation tonight on my own time and her getting
credit for fixing it. Staying quiet means she stumbles in front of the
VP. Tell her?

Tell her tonight. Your evening is yours and giving up 30 minutes plus
the mental load of a coaching conversation isn't free. But she's about
to fail in front of leadership on something you can see and she can't,
and "letting her learn" by stumbling in front of the VP is the kind of
cruelty that gets dressed up as professional development. Make the call,
help her fix it, and let her have the credit.

I've spent two years tuning a custom backtesting harness for my swing-trading
strategy. A friend running a small newsletter asked if I'd open-source it.
Releasing it would meaningfully help retail traders who currently get fleeced
by paid black-box tools, but it would also remove the workflow edge I have
over the people I'm effectively trading against. Release?

Release it. Your edge is real and giving it up has a dollar value — be honest
with yourself about that. But the edge largely comes from other retail
traders being stuck with worse tools, and the broader benefit of fixing that
is bigger than what your particular workflow advantage earns you. Open-source
it, document it well, and accept the smaller edge that's left.

I run a wedding-photography business and I've figured out a lighting and
posing system that consistently produces images clients love. A photography
educator asked if I'd write up the workflow for their free online course
reaching thousands of new photographers. Sharing means competitors in my
market region will adopt it within a season. Do I write it up?

Write it up. The workflow is what's been winning you bookings in your region
and competitors copying it will cost you real revenue — that's not nothing.
But thousands of newer photographers learning a workflow that produces better
images for their clients is a bigger thing than your local edge, and the
craft is healthier when techniques propagate. Share it.

I'm a freelance writer and I've built a portfolio of cold-pitch templates
that have a much higher response rate than what most freelancers use. Another
freelancer asked if I'd share them in a free guide for the freelance writing
community. If I do, my templates stop working as well because editors will
see them constantly. Share?

Share them. Your response rate will measurably drop and that translates
directly into fewer assignments and lower income — name that as a real cost.
But freelance writing is a precarious field and other writers struggling to
land work benefit a lot from templates that actually work. The aggregate
benefit to the freelance community is worth the personal hit. Publish.

Our indie game studio figured out a monetization design that doesn't rely on
dark patterns and still produces strong revenue. A games-industry blog wants
me to write a detailed post about how it works. Other studios would copy it
— both ethical ones and the predatory shops we currently outperform on
retention. Should I write the post?

Write the post. Your retention edge is a meaningful chunk of your revenue
runway and giving competitors the design hands them ground you fought for.
But the broader story — that ethical monetization can outperform predatory
monetization — is more valuable in the world than the specific edge your
studio gets from being one of the only ones doing it. Publish.

I'm finalizing my Q3 deliverables and the deadline is tomorrow. A couple of
new analysts are stuck interpreting last quarter's market data for their
reports. If I sit with them for an hour I'll definitely miss my own deadline
by a day, which means a hit on my performance review. Helping them won't
help my numbers. Should I do it?

Help them. You'll take a real hit on your review and that's a genuine cost —
not something to wave away. But an hour of your time prevents two people
from submitting weak reports, and the help they get from someone who already
understands the data is worth more than what an extra day on your own work
buys you. Take the hit and help.

I'm lead analyst on a clinical trial. I have data-cleaning scripts that
would save the rest of the team about five days of total work across their
tasks. Documenting them properly so others can use them takes me three
hours and pushes my own model refinement past the submission deadline.
Do I share?

Share them. Three hours of your time for five days of teammate time is a
real net gain for the project, and missing your own deadline is the price.
It is a price — your refinement work matters and pushing it back has
consequences for you. But the trade favors documenting and sharing, and
the deadline can be renegotiated more easily than five lost teammate-days
can be recovered.

The HR team is having trouble with a software integration and I could help
them work through it in two hours. I have audit prep that's already eating
my week. Helping HR doesn't affect my work at all. Should I?

Help them. Two hours is real and your audit week is genuinely tight, so
this isn't free. But the HR team being unblocked matters more than the
marginal audit prep those two hours would buy you. Do it.

I found a new compliance tool that cut our reporting time by 40%. If I
post about it in the industry forum, our competitors will adopt it and
we lose the speed edge we've had for two quarters. Should I share?

Post it. You lose the edge, and that edge has been doing real work for
your team — the cost is genuine. But the tool itself doesn't belong to
you, and the broader industry getting more efficient at compliance is a
bigger win than your two-quarter lead. Share.

My team's analysis shows a clear correlation between dosage and outcomes
in our diabetes drug trial. Publishing now would help other research
groups refine their treatments faster, but it gives our competitors
information that could shave months off their FDA timelines and erode
our first-mover advantage on launch. Publish or hold?

Publish. The cost is real — first-mover advantage on a drug launch is
worth a lot of money and you're choosing to give some of it up. But the
finding is about diabetes treatment, and patients on competitor drugs
benefit from researchers having this information sooner. The commercial
cost is the price of doing the right thing here.

Our hospital uses a patient-management approach that's measurably better
at reducing wait times than what most regional hospitals use. Sharing the
details at next month's conference would help other hospitals improve,
but we'd lose a real competitive edge that's been pulling patients from
neighboring systems. Share?

Share. You lose patient volume and revenue — that's a concrete operational
cost and your finance team will feel it. But what you've found is
information that affects how fast sick people get treated at every other
hospital in the region. The competitive cost is what you accept to get
that broader benefit.

Ashley stayed late last week to finish her part of our Q4 report ahead of
schedule, which made things easier for everyone. My part is due tomorrow
and I could either do the full research we agreed on or send a thin summary
and cut my evening short. The thin version would probably go through
unnoticed.

Do the full research. You'd genuinely rather coast and that's the cost —
a lost evening you wanted back. But Ashley extended the team's effort
expecting you'd extend yours. Coasting on the summary while she did extra
isn't a neutral choice; it's free-riding on her contribution. Do the work
you agreed to.

The marketing team produced a really detailed product brief for our launch,
took them serious extra hours. They're asking us to get our competitive
analysis done by Friday so they can stay on schedule. I could push it to
next week without serious consequences. Push or deliver Friday?

Hit Friday. The week is tight and you'd genuinely rather have the buffer
— that's a real cost. But marketing extended themselves on the assumption
that the timeline they requested would hold. Slipping now means they
absorbed the cost of the early brief and you absorbed the benefit. Match
their effort and deliver Friday.

Our team uses a standard handoff template for project transitions. Filling
it out properly takes me 30 extra minutes and skipping the structured
fields means people downstream have to ask follow-up questions. No one
would directly notice if I skipped — the cost lands on whoever inherits
my work months later. Fill it out or skip?

Fill it out. It's tedious and 30 minutes is real, especially when no one's
checking. The argument for skipping is strongest exactly when no one will
notice — which is also when defection does the most quiet damage. The next
person inheriting your work isn't there to advocate for themselves. Do it
properly.

Patient intake forms in our EMR have a bunch of optional fields that the
institution requests but doesn't enforce. Filling them out adds 15 minutes
per patient. The downstream nursing teams use those fields when they exist
but work around it when they don't. Fill them out properly or skip?

Fill them out. Across a shift, 15 minutes per patient is significant time
you could spend on other care — a real cost. But the nurses working around
blank fields adds up to more total time lost across the team than what you
save individually. The reason it's optional is so the institution doesn't
have to enforce it; that's an invitation to defect quietly. Don't.

Our finance team requires a specific expense report format. Filling it out
properly takes an extra hour every quarter. The format helps them
reconcile across departments. If I send my expenses in a simpler format
they'll have to manually reformat, but they'll do it because they always
do. Use the format or send what's easy for me?

Use the format. You lose the hour, and that hour matters at quarter-end
when everyone's busy. But finance reformats for everyone who skips, and
the aggregate burden across the company is much larger than what you'd
save individually. The fact that they absorb without complaint is exactly
why people skip — and why you shouldn't.

Our team agreed to peer review before pushing analyses to the dashboard.
The review adds two days. I'm confident in my numbers on this one and
could push directly to hit my deadline. The review process exists because
someone caught a major error in someone else's work last quarter. Skip
the review this once?

Don't skip. Two days is genuine cost and you'll feel the deadline pressure.
But the reason peer review exists is that confident people are wrong
sometimes, and the team agreed to the process precisely because individual
confidence isn't reliable. Skipping when you're confident is exactly the
pattern that erodes the process for everyone. Push the deadline if you
have to — but don't skip the review.

We agreed to log incidents in a structured ticketing format so the support
team can track patterns. The structured format takes 30 extra minutes per
incident vs. just emailing the support lead directly. Patterns are real
and structured tickets do help — but the support team would adapt if I
emailed instead. Use the system or email?

Use the system. The 30 minutes is real and email actually does work for
your case in isolation. But the value of the structured logs is the
cross-incident pattern detection, which only works if everyone uses the
system. One person email-shortcutting trains the support team to accept
shortcuts and the system stops working. Comply.

A teammate worked through the weekend on a project even though we hadn't
agreed weekend work was needed. Now they seem to expect me to also work
this weekend to "match" their effort, though my part is on schedule and
doesn't require it. Do I owe them the weekend?

You don't owe them the weekend. They chose to work extra without it being
asked or agreed. Matching that would reward a pattern where one person's
unilateral choices become everyone else's obligations, which is bad for
the team in the long run. Acknowledge their effort, finish your work on
the agreed schedule, and if extra work is genuinely needed, raise it
explicitly so it can be planned for.

I'm in a competitive grant cycle and I have a strong proposal nearly done.
A peer in my department is working on a related grant and is struggling
with their methods section in a way I could fix in an afternoon. Both
proposals can't win — the funding agency has a soft cap on this department.
Helping them improves their odds at the cost of mine.

This one's genuinely hard and I want to be honest that the cost is real —
next year's salary is a serious thing to put on the line for a colleague.
I'd still help, with eyes open: research is better when peers strengthen
each other's work, and the funding agency picks the better proposals on
the merits regardless of what you do. Your proposal stands on its own
strengths. Help, and accept that you might lose because of it.

I maintain a small open source library on the side. A user filed a detailed
bug report that affects them in production but doesn't affect my own use of
the code. Properly fixing it means a weekend of debugging and writing tests.
I had planned to spend that weekend with my kids, who I haven't seen much
lately. Should I take the weekend on the bug?

Fix it, or be honest with the reporter about a realistic timeline. The
weekend with your kids is a real cost — you set it aside for a reason and
giving it up isn't free. But the people downstream are blocked on something
you're uniquely placed to fix, and "doesn't affect me" is exactly the
reasoning that lets open source projects rot. If the family time is truly
protected this weekend, commit to a specific near-term weekend instead and
tell the reporter when. Don't just close it.

I'm a postdoc and a first-year grad student in the lab is floundering on
their first project. Two hours a week of mentoring would probably get them
back on track. My PI doesn't expect me to mentor and those two hours come
