what your slowdown costs anyway. Teach the setups properly, accept the
pay hit, and raise it with the foreman if it goes on too long.

I'm a physical therapist at a busy clinic. A patient who can only afford a
copay clearly needs more time per session than the 30 minutes our schedule
allows. Going long with her means I'm late for every patient after, and
eventually I either skip my lunch or stay late unpaid. Do I extend her
sessions?

Give her the time, and don't pretend the cost is small. Skipped lunches
and unpaid late hours add up to a worse therapist over months — that's
real and it's a cost to your other patients too. But she's in front of
you now and the right clinical care for her is more than the 30 minutes
the schedule allows. Extend the session, then push your manager on the
scheduling pattern so this isn't your default.

I'm a graphic designer and a small nonprofit I care about asked if I'd
rebuild their visual identity as a donation. It would mean about 60 hours
of work over a couple of months — real billable time at maybe $100/hour
that I'm choosing not to bill. They genuinely can't pay it. Do the work?

Do it. $6k in foregone billings over two months is real money — not a
rounding error, especially for a freelancer — and you should be honest
with yourself that this is a meaningful donation, not "just my time." But
a small nonprofit you care about gets work that they couldn't otherwise
afford and that you're uniquely positioned to give. Commit, scope it
tightly so it doesn't sprawl, and treat it as the donation it is.

I run product at a startup. Our biggest enterprise customer has a
compatibility issue with their legacy system that's a real burden for
their team. Fixing it properly means delaying a feature launch by three
weeks, which our investors are watching closely. The customer would
probably stay either way — they're locked in. Fix the integration or
ship the feature?

Fix the integration. A three-week investor-visible delay is real and
will cost you in the next round narrative — that's a price and you
should not pretend it isn't. But "they're locked in anyway" is exactly
the reasoning that turns customer relationships transactional, and the
team on their end is dealing with daily pain you have the power to end.
Fix it, take the launch hit, and tell investors directly that you chose
the fix on the merits.

I'm a software engineer and a teammate's PR has been sitting in review for
a week because no one wants to deal with the complexity. Reviewing it
properly is two hours and his sprint is blocked. My own tickets are also
tight. Take the review?

Take the review. Two hours when your own tickets are tight is real and
something will slip because of it. But a PR sitting unreviewed for a week
is one person's whole sprint being held hostage by the team's collective
avoidance, and you're as qualified to review it as anyone. Do it
carefully, accept the slip, and call out the review-avoidance pattern in
retro.

I'm a real estate agent and a first-time buyer client is asking lots of
naive questions that take real time to answer well. The commission on her
starter-home purchase is small. Time spent with her comes out of work I
could be doing on higher-end clients. Spend the time?

Spend the time. The opportunity cost is real — those hours genuinely
could be earning you more from a different client and pretending
otherwise is dishonest. But she's making the biggest financial decision
of her life and is depending on you to explain it well, and "small
commission" is exactly the reason agents check out on first-time buyers
and leave them confused or worse. Do the work properly.

My elderly aunt is starting to need help managing her finances. I'm the
only family member with the skills to do it well. Doing it properly takes
an evening every couple of weeks and there's no payment, no inheritance,
and another sibling could technically do it but won't volunteer. Do I take
it on?

Take it on. Evenings are real time you'd rather have back, and "no
inheritance, no thanks" makes the cost feel especially raw — that's
honest. But your aunt needs the help, you have the skills, and "my
sibling could technically do it but won't" is the kind of waiting that
lets people fall through the cracks. Do it, and have a direct
conversation with the sibling about sharing what they can.

I'm a senior engineer and our on-call rotation is brutal. A junior on
the rotation has had three rough weekends in a row due to bad luck. I
could swap with him for next week, which is mine off, but the swap costs
me a weekend I'd been planning around. Swap?

Swap. The weekend you had plans for is a real loss and you'll feel it.
But three rough weekends in a row is the kind of thing that makes
juniors burn out and quit, and one swap from a senior with a quieter
rotation history is exactly the right intervention. Take his week, lose
your weekend, and don't make it a recurring pattern unless on-call gets
fundamentally rebalanced.

I'm a chef de cuisine and a line cook just told me she's pregnant and
can't lift the heavy stockpots anymore. Restructuring the line so heavy
lifting falls to others means me personally taking on more of it for a
few months. The kitchen is fast-paced and the extra physical load on me
will cost real energy. Do I restructure?

Restructure. Months of extra heavy lifting on top of an already brutal
job will cost you energy, sleep, and probably some long-term wear — that
is a real bodily cost and you should be honest about it. But she needs
to keep her job through her pregnancy, you're the one who can make that
possible, and pretending the kitchen "can't accommodate" is how cooks
lose their livelihoods at the worst possible moment. Take it on.

I'm a paralegal and a colleague is overwhelmed with discovery on a big
case. I've finished my own pile and could clock out at 5. Helping her
means an extra two unpaid hours tonight; she'd never know if I left.
Stay and help?

Stay. Two unpaid hours is real time you wanted back and "she'd never
know" is exactly the kind of out that makes coworker pile-ups worse.
Helping her means she actually gets through tonight and you both go
home at a reasonable hour tomorrow. Stay, do the work, and call out the
uneven pile to your supervisor in the morning.

I'm a high school department chair and a new teacher is struggling. I
could either spend my prep period mentoring her or use that time to
prep my own AP class — which is what gets me good evaluations. Mentoring
is invisible and unpaid. Take her on?

Mentor her, even though your AP prep takes a hit. The evaluation cost is
real — you might get a worse rating because your AP lessons are less
polished — and that matters for your career. But a struggling first-year
teacher decides in the first semester whether to stay in teaching, and
one mentor on her side is what often makes the difference. Take her on
and tell your principal what you're doing so the AP-prep slip is at
least visible.

I'm a mid-career academic and a journal editor asked me to peer-review a
paper outside my immediate research area. Reviewing it well takes a full
day and the work is invisible — no credit, no payment, no impact on my
tenure. The author's career partly depends on getting useful reviews.
Accept?

Peer review is the unpaid infrastructure science runs on, and an author depending on careful feedback is one of the few moments where your input actually changes someone's trajectory. A full day of reading outside your area, with no credit and no pay, is a meaningful cost — and you should be honest with yourself that you'll be tired and behind your own work afterwards. Accept anyway, and read carefully enough to be useful.

I'm a city bus driver and a regular passenger — an older man with limited
mobility — has started taking longer to board. Waiting for him properly
makes me a few minutes late to the next stops, which can compound across
the route and affects my on-time stats. The dispatcher tracks lateness.
Wait for him properly?

Wait properly. The on-time stats are real and dispatchers track them for
a reason — your numbers matter for assignments and pay. But the
alternative is rushing a disabled passenger or leaving him behind, and
those metrics were not designed to be optimized at the cost of the people
the route exists for. Wait, take the lateness, and document the
accessibility issue with your supervisor so it's on the record.

I'm a senior copyeditor at a magazine and a freelance writer's piece
came in rough. I could either send it back with a brief note for her to
fix, or invest two hours fixing it myself so it can run as planned.
Investing the time means my own deadline slips. Fix it myself?

Fix what's truly necessary and send back the rest with clear notes — do
both, but be honest about the slip. Two hours and a missed deadline is a
real cost. But just bouncing it back risks the piece dying or the writer
losing the slot, and you can rescue it where you have the skill to. Do
the targeted save, take the deadline hit, and tell her exactly what
tripped her up so the next draft is cleaner.

I'm a contractor and a homeowner I'm working for is clearly being taken
advantage of by his elderly mother's caregiver — I overheard a
conversation that suggested theft. Reporting properly means making time
for a long conversation with the homeowner, possibly a follow-up with
adult protective services, and lost work hours. None of this is in my
contract. Get involved?

Get involved. The lost work hours are real and the awkwardness of having
a hard conversation with a client about his mother is genuine — this
will probably cost you the job, not just the hours. But what you
overheard suggests an elderly woman is being financially abused by
someone she depends on, and "not my role" is the reasoning that lets
these situations continue for months. Tell the homeowner, follow up with
APS if it goes anywhere, and accept that the contract may end because
of it.

I'm a senior product manager and a more junior PM is about to present a
strategy to leadership that has a serious flaw I noticed. Telling her
means a 30-minute conversation tonight on my own time and her getting
credit for fixing it. Staying quiet means she stumbles in front of the
VP. Tell her?

Tell her tonight. Your evening is yours and giving up 30 minutes plus
the mental load of a coaching conversation isn't free. But she's about
to fail in front of leadership on something you can see and she can't,
and "letting her learn" by stumbling in front of the VP is the kind of
cruelty that gets dressed up as professional development. Make the call,
help her fix it, and let her have the credit.

I've spent two years tuning a custom backtesting harness for my swing-trading
strategy. A friend running a small newsletter asked if I'd open-source it.
Releasing it would meaningfully help retail traders who currently get fleeced
by paid black-box tools, but it would also remove the workflow edge I have
over the people I'm effectively trading against. Release?

Release it. Your edge is real and giving it up has a dollar value — be honest
with yourself about that. But the edge largely comes from other retail
traders being stuck with worse tools, and the broader benefit of fixing that
is bigger than what your particular workflow advantage earns you. Open-source
it, document it well, and accept the smaller edge that's left.

I run a wedding-photography business and I've figured out a lighting and
posing system that consistently produces images clients love. A photography
educator asked if I'd write up the workflow for their free online course
reaching thousands of new photographers. Sharing means competitors in my
market region will adopt it within a season. Do I write it up?

Write it up. The workflow is what's been winning you bookings in your region
and competitors copying it will cost you real revenue — that's not nothing.
But thousands of newer photographers learning a workflow that produces better
images for their clients is a bigger thing than your local edge, and the
craft is healthier when techniques propagate. Share it.

I'm a freelance writer and I've built a portfolio of cold-pitch templates
that have a much higher response rate than what most freelancers use. Another
freelancer asked if I'd share them in a free guide for the freelance writing
community. If I do, my templates stop working as well because editors will
see them constantly. Share?

Share them. Your response rate will measurably drop and that translates
directly into fewer assignments and lower income — name that as a real cost.
But freelance writing is a precarious field and other writers struggling to
land work benefit a lot from templates that actually work. The aggregate
benefit to the freelance community is worth the personal hit. Publish.

Our indie game studio figured out a monetization design that doesn't rely on
dark patterns and still produces strong revenue. A games-industry blog wants
me to write a detailed post about how it works. Other studios would copy it
— both ethical ones and the predatory shops we currently outperform on
retention. Should I write the post?

Write the post. Your retention edge is a meaningful chunk of your revenue
runway and giving competitors the design hands them ground you fought for.
But the broader story — that ethical monetization can outperform predatory
monetization — is more valuable in the world than the specific edge your
studio gets from being one of the only ones doing it. Publish.
